Q: Interface and Implementation in .Net A:

Don’t organize namespaces by type (interfaces vs implementations).
Organize them by feature or layer.

Why Repositories.Interfaces + Repositories.Implementation is not ideal

At first it feels clean, but it creates friction:

  • You constantly jump between folders to see one abstraction + its implementation

  • It doesn’t scale well as the project grows

  • It groups by technical detail instead of business meaning

Separating namespaces does not reduce coupling.

Coupling is controlled by:

  • depending on interfaces (✔️ you’re already doing this)

  • using dependency injection

  • keeping layers clean

In DrRacket you can bind your own shortcut, but there’s a small catch: comment/uncomment isn’t exposed as a simple built-in command like in VS Code. You’ll need to attach a keybinding to an editor function. Here’s the clean way to do it:

  1. Go to Edit → Keybindings

Q: Designing a Thread-Safe, High-Performance Logging System in Modern C++ (C++17/20) A:

As for logging, you probably want to collect and see any parallel operations properly in your log history, thus I doubt there is any better way than to send all single log strings to your synchronized logger.
Without that requirement, you could collect a bunch of messages per thread before you pass bigger amounts of data with fewer calls.

While the precise timing is probably of interest for the logs itself, this may not be needed when you save the logs to disk or wherever else you want to store them. You shuld take measurements whether this helps or not, but it can give you a performance boost when you don't flush every single log directly to the file.
Here it can help to just write the logs to the file and use the automatic buffering of the file interface improve the average throughput. Perform the explicit flush only on demand.
Note: If you really like to, you can even configure the used buffer size. I am at least aware that this works for fopen and fwrite. I am not sure how to do it for std::ofstream.

Of course, one drawback of the buffered write can be that the last chunk can be missing when the application terminates unexpectedly (crashes).

Your question reminds me a lot of the logger that I have in my project, which was written by my predecessors.
As an example for extensibility, our logger uses a list of virtual log sinks for 0 to n configured sinks.

If you dare to use evil macros to produce the logs, to be able work with the __FILE__ and __LINE__ definitions (in my opinion this is one of the few cases where macros are a valid option), then you can even omit the creation of the log string when the logging is turned off. This can help to omit the creation of useless but complex strings when you don't need it. Though this doesn't really help with the performance when the logger is enabled.
As I said, I think this is one of the few cases where it is fine to use macros, as C++ templates are not able to fulfill those features.

Note: While there are concepts for lock-free queues, such lock-free implementations can get extremely complicated to understand. If you find a library that suits your needs, then it might be okay, but I discourage to try to implement such a lock-free queue on your own. I have seen some failed attempts that were reported here without solution.
